title: Does adding modular predicates preserve decidable first-order definability?
formal: For every effective first-order fragment \(\mathcal F\) satisfying the closure conditions below, does decidability of \(\mathcal F[<]\)-definability of regular finite-word languages imply decidability of \(\mathcal F[<,\mathrm{MOD}]\)-definability? Each decision algorithm takes a finite alphabet and a deterministic finite automaton as input; the fragment is fixed.
why: This asks whether adding elementary arithmetic tests to word logics preserves the ability to recognize their expressive power algorithmically. A general transfer theorem would replace separate definability arguments for many fragments; a counterexample would identify limits of that expectation even for effective, substitution-closed syntax.
status_note: The 2013 source poses a general research direction. The precise effective-fragment universe above is an explicitly documented editorial variant using later standard closure conditions. Follow-up results checked through 13 September 2026 establish selected-fragment and stronger-premise transfer theorems; no resolution of this exact universal membership-only implication was located in the bounded check. The original source alone does not certify the status of every possible formalization of “fragment”.

progress.text: Dartois and Paperman decide first-order definability with two variables and modular predicates, and ask the general fragment-transfer question in Section 7.
Place, Ramanathan and Weil establish transfer results for separation and covering with the stated local-enrichment hypotheses; Section 3.2 gives an abstract fragment framework.

category_assignment.reason: The question is decidability of regular-language definability after adding modular numerical predicates to a logical fragment over words.

importance.reason: A broad but model-sensitive meta-decidability question connecting word logic and algebraic language classification; the explicit fragment framework makes its intended transfer claim testable.

sentences: The input is a deterministic finite automaton for a regular language of finite words.
The base decision problem asks whether some sentence in a fixed first-order fragment defines that language.
The enriched fragment may also inspect position and word-length congruences for any finite choice of moduli.
The card asks whether base decidability always transfers, using an explicitly specified effective and substitution-closed fragment framework.
Known transfer theorems for stronger separation problems or additional local predicates do not directly establish this membership-only implication.

definitions: A word \(w=a_1\cdots a_n\) over a finite nonempty alphabet \(A\) is the finite structure on positions \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with position equality, order \(<\), and a unary letter predicate \(Q_a(i)\) for each \(a\in A\), true exactly when \(a_i=a\). Empty words have no positions. First-order formulas have Boolean connectives and quantifiers over positions only. The modular signature adds unary predicates \(M_{d,r}(i)\) meaning \(i\equiv r\pmod d\), and nullary predicates \(N_{d,r}\) meaning \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), for all integers \(d\geq1\) and \(0\leq r<d\). A formula uses finitely many of them, but there is no global modulus bound. These are position and length congruences, not quantifiers counting the number of positions satisfying a subformula. A fragment fixes either finitely many variable names or a countable list of names, and for every finite relational signature \(S\) specifies a set \(\mathcal F[S]\) of first-order formulas using those names. It contains all quantifier-free formulas on those variables and signatures, is closed under conjunction and disjunction, and is closed under quantifier-free substitution of relation atoms by formulas with the same available free variables, with bound variables renamed to avoid capture. Effectiveness here means one terminating procedure decides syntactic membership of a finite formula in \(\mathcal F[S]\) when its finite signature and formula are given. The names and arities of predicates and modular integers have ordinary finite encodings. For a signature with infinitely many available modular predicates, membership is read on the finite signature actually used. The notation \(\mathcal F[<]\) includes the letter and equality predicates, and \(\mathcal F[<,\mathrm{MOD}]\) also permits the modular predicates just defined. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is an explicit finite state set, initial state, final-state subset and total transition table on \(A\); it recognizes a regular language \(L\subseteq A^*\). Definability asks whether some sentence in the specified fragment has exactly language \(L\), for all finite words. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine halting on every DFA/alphabet input. Its program may depend on the fixed fragment; no uniform transformation from base deciders to enriched deciders or running-time bound is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every effective fragment satisfying the specified closure conditions. Alternatively define a particular such fragment, prove its effectiveness and closure properties in Lean, give a Lean-verified algorithm for its base definability problem, and prove in Lean that the enriched definability problem is undecidable. Results about satisfiability, fixed moduli, separation given as an additional oracle, or only selected standard fragments do not decide this full implication.

context_blocks.text: The 2013 paper poses a general transfer question for fragments without providing one formal universe of admissible fragment descriptions. Editorial convention: the target above uses the quantifier-free-substitution closure framework made explicit in the 2019 follow-up literature, and additionally requires decidable syntax. This states a concrete transfer proposition; it is not presented as a verbatim formal theorem from the original concluding paragraph.

Adding congruence tests can increase expressive power while preserving regularity. For example, a nullary length predicate can require the whole word to have even length, and a unary predicate can restrict which letters occur at positions of a given parity. The question concerns whether a supplied regular language can be described at all, not whether an individual sentence has a model.

The 2013 theorem establishes decidability for two-variable first-order logic with modular predicates. Two-variable logic allows reusing two position-variable names under nested quantifiers. This important instance does not imply the universal transfer proposition for all admissible fragments.

Place, Ramanathan and Weil develop a generic transfer theorem for separation and covering when the underlying language classes already include an appropriate enrichment by local predicates such as successor. Their statement both assumes a stronger decision problem and uses structural hypotheses beyond the bare decidable-membership premise here.

Separation takes two regular languages and asks for a language of the fragment containing the first and disjoint from the second. Definability is the special case where the pair is a language and its complement. Consequently, decidable definability alone does not supply the separation algorithm assumed by those transfer results.

There is also a difference between allowing any finite collection of moduli in the defining sentence and fixing that collection in advance. The sentence may need a modulus that is absent from the input automaton’s syntax. A proof for each fixed modular signature must justify how it handles this unbounded existential choice before settling the stated problem.
